To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the maximum capacity of a clustered network scales as N ^{1−1/α}, and that this scaling exponent can be achieved with a throughput scaling as N ^{1-1/α}.

the capacity per node scales as the square root of node density, and that the optimal strategy depends on whether the node density is below or above a certain threshold, and on the number of hops that the signal travels in the network.
the maximum throughput scales like the square root of the number of nodes for all operational regimes except for one.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the analysis of the information-theoretic capacity in the following scenarios: (1) a network of randomly located nodes, (2) a network of clustered nodes, (3) a network with a single base station, (4) a network with multiple base stations, and (5) a network in which nodes are randomly located in a finite area and communicate via a relay station located in a remote region.

the following three main topics: (i) the derivation of a new class of shot-noise Cox processes that are relevant for the analysis of clustered random networks; (ii) the characterization of the capacity of such networks; (iii) the design of communication strategies that allow to achieve the capacity.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in the case of a doubly stochastic Cox process the capacity of the network scales as N^(2/3), where N is the total number of nodes in the network.
the maximum capacity of a clustered ad hoc network scales like the square root of the average number of clusters per node, which is the square root of its density.

in the case of a doubly stochastic Cox process the maximum theoretical capacity is achieved by the communication strategy we devised, and the throughput achieved by this strategy is the maximum possible throughput.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the case of clustered networks, there is no loss of optimality in terms of capacity scaling exponents, even when nodes are clustered.
, in the case of a clustered ad hoc network, the capacity scaling law is determined by the number of clusters and not the total node density.
the capacity scaling of clustered random networks depends on the relative strengths of clustering, spatial density and node transmission range.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of clustering in the spatial distribution of nodes does not significantly impact the scaling laws of the network capacity.
in clustered networks the capacity scaling exponent depends on the cluster size distribution.

, for a given network density, the capacity of clustered random ad hoc networks is always larger than that of the corresponding Poisson networks, and that the capacity gap can be as large as the order of magnitude.
